title: depression
thesis: A shared spelling moves through several kinds of descent. Its largest book-frequency peak belongs to an economic crisis period, not to a clinical count. Across books, its surrounding language changes before its spelling does.
closingFinding: This is not one straight path from sadness to sickness. Depression is a branching word: mood, market, pressure, landscape, weather and diagnosis share its spelling without sharing one meaning.

chapters.title: A downward word before a reliable curve.
chapters.deck: The early record locates several senses; it does not support a continuous frequency story.
chapters.visibleCaveat: Lexical-source dates are sense-history anchors, not first-use claims or corpus rates.

summary.title: SIX LEXICAL ANCHORS
summary.accessibleSummary: Six secondary lexical-source anchors mark astronomical, emotional, physical, economic, meteorological and clinical branches from around 1400 to 1905.
summary.caveat: Anchor spacing is chronological only; it does not encode amount.

detail.title: WHAT EACH DATE CAN SAY
detail.accessibleSummary: Each date is a secondary lexical-source anchor with a named semantic category and confidence state; none is shown as a first-use claim.
detail.caveat: These are retained secondary lexical records, not a comparable historical corpus.

chapters.title: A new word enters print; melancholy still leads.
chapters.deck: Depression becomes continuously visible in books, but it is not yet the dominant historical neighbour for low mood.
chapters.visibleCaveat: The comparison measures printed forms in one corpus, not interchangeable meanings.

summary.title: PERIOD AVERAGE
summary.accessibleSummary: From 1800 through 1873, depression averages 6.28 and melancholy 20.20 appearances per million corpus words; melancholy is about 3.2 times the depression rate.
summary.caveat: Both bars share a zero baseline and the same denominator.

detail.title: THREE HISTORICAL NEIGHBORS
detail.accessibleSummary: Nine-year centered annual means keep depression below melancholy through this early print period; anxiety is shown as a distinct neighbouring term.
detail.caveat: Melancholy and anxiety are comparative forms, not counted senses of depression.

chapters.title: Depression crosses melancholy; market language gains weight.
chapters.deck: Its printed visibility stays above melancholy from 1874 onward. That is a visibility crossover, not semantic replacement.
chapters.visibleCaveat: A sustained frequency crossover is not evidence of a semantic replacement.

summary.title: A SUSTAINED CROSSOVER
summary.accessibleSummary: A nine-year centered average for depression stays above melancholy for twenty consecutive years beginning in 1874.
summary.caveat: This compares forms in print, not the meanings of all uses.

annotations.detail: first year of the sustained visibility crossover

detail.title: MARKET PHRASES, SEPARATE BRANCH
detail.accessibleSummary: Business depression, financial depression and economic depression share one zero-to-3.5 scale from 1874 through 1928.
detail.caveat: Phrase frequency is not an estimate of the share of meanings carried by the core word.

chapters.title: 1932: the highest peak is not a diagnosis.
chapters.deck: The core word rises sharply during the Great Depression period alongside independent economic phrase series.
chapters.visibleCaveat: Economic timing is contextual evidence, not proof that every book use is economic.

summary.title: THE HIGH POINT
summary.accessibleSummary: Depression reaches 43.33 appearances per million corpus words in 1932. All eleven raw annual values from 1929 through 1939 are shown.
summary.caveat: The lollipops share a zero baseline; 1932 is directly marked.

detail.title: ECONOMIC PHRASES IN CONTEXT
detail.accessibleSummary: Economic, business and financial depression are separate low-scale phrase series. The NBER 1929–1933 contraction band is contextual, not causal proof.
detail.caveat: The NBER event is shown beside phrase series; it does not classify individual book uses.

events.label: NBER 1929–1933 CONTRACTION
events.role: contextual economic event; not lexical evidence

chapters.title: The peak recedes; diagnostic language stays marginal.
chapters.deck: The broad word remains visible after the economic peak, while clinical labels have not yet formed a durable high-frequency band.
chapters.visibleCaveat: A low phrase rate does not measure disease prevalence or diagnostic practice.

summary.title: TWO POST-CRISIS PLATFORMS
summary.accessibleSummary: Depression averages 13.33 appearances per million corpus words in 1940–1959 and 11.10 in 1960–1979.
summary.caveat: Both platform bars share a zero baseline.

detail.title: LABELS BEFORE THEIR LATER RISE
detail.accessibleSummary: Clinical depression, major depression and depressive disorder stay in much lower-frequency bands. A 0.1-per-million reference is marked separately on each scale.
detail.caveat: These phrase rates do not project current diagnostic definitions back onto earlier decades.

chapters.title: Diagnostic labels rise; the shared word stays multiple.
chapters.deck: Clinical phrases become more visible after the early 1980s. The core word still names more than diagnosis.
chapters.visibleCaveat: Diagnostic phrase frequency is not a count of diagnoses, people or public-health prevalence.

summary.title: A DURABLE LABEL BAND
summary.accessibleSummary: Major depression and depressive disorder first remain above 0.1 appearances per million under the nine-year, five-consecutive-year rule in 1983. Clinical depression uses a 0.01 threshold because it does not cross 0.1 in that period.
summary.caveat: Every dense annual mark represents a retained yearly value; threshold logic uses nine-year centered means.

detail.title: A MODERN NEIGHBOUR, NOT A SYNONYM
detail.accessibleSummary: In the 2010s, depression averages 23.03 and anxiety 26.15 appearances per million corpus words. In 2022 they are 22.86 and 32.34 respectively.
detail.caveat: Anxiety is adjacent in this comparison, not a replacement or subset of depression.

sources.label: Google Books Ngram Viewer
sources.use: Annual English book-frequency series; stored fractions are converted to appearances per million corpus words.

sources.label: Lexical-source attestation records
sources.use: Sense-history anchors only; not a continuous corpus or first-use record.

sources.label: NBER US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions
sources.use: Economic event context only; not lexical frequency evidence.

sources.label: MeSH / NCBI
sources.use: Controlled-vocabulary context only; not general-language frequency evidence.

methods: Every charted book rate is the stored annual Google Books Ngram fraction multiplied by 1,000,000. The source file is the English corpus, 1500–2022, with source smoothing set to zero.
Period values are arithmetic means of every annual value in the labelled inclusive range. Raw annual plots remain unsmoothed unless the chart itself is labelled as a nine-year centered mean.

The 1874 crossover requires depression to exceed melancholy on a nine-year centered average for twenty consecutive years. Modern thresholds require five consecutive years above the stated rate using the same centered mean.
The 03A wheel compares business depression, financial depression and economic depression on one shared 0–3.5-per-million scale. Every phrase retains all 66 annual positions from 1874 through 1939.
Economic-event dates and controlled-vocabulary dates are contextual layers. They are not normalized with book-frequency values and do not prove causal relationships.
caveats: A single depression frequency series is not sense-classified. No chart treats emotional, economic, physical or clinical senses as shares of one whole.
Early Ngram values are sparse and potentially noisy. The first chapter therefore uses lexical anchors rather than a continuous early-frequency plot.
Phrase frequency is not a count of diagnoses, people, disease prevalence, economic output or the share of meanings carried by the core word.
rights: Google Books Ngram Viewer data and all linked institutional sources remain subject to their own terms and attribution requirements.
Words Over Time presents derived rates, small rendered excerpts of source metadata, and links for research navigation; it does not republish source corpora.
